extracted.intended_audience: short fiction writers looking to find markets and get published
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on researching short-story markets, choosing where to submit, and how to write/submit stories that stand out to editors and slush readers. Covers practical discovery tools, factors to weigh (audience, pay, shininess), and craft/submission strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to find short-story markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate market lists and examples of where award-winning fiction was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregated lists such as The Submission Grinder, Duotrope, or Ralan’s; look at anthologies and collections of award-winning short fiction (e.g., Nebula Award Showcase) to see where pieces were originally published. These sources let you find current markets, but be aware markets churn frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate markets by three priorities: audience, pay rate, shininess
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose markets based on (1) audience size, (2) pay rate, and (3) how 'shiny' (prestigious/desirable) the market is for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which of these matters most for your career stage or immediate goals. Audience affects exposure; pay rate affects income; shininess affects prestige and personal satisfaction. The relative importance can change over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match market editorial focus to your taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Target markets whose editorial focus and published stories align with the kinds of stories you like and want to be alongside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read current short fiction and notice which markets you gravitate to. Being excited about the other stories in a market is a sign it's a good fit for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and study contemporary short fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly read current short fiction to understand market styles and to develop instincts about what grabs you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading helps you discover markets, learn their styles, and hone your reader-instincts which you should trust when writing. The hosts recommend reading award collections as part of this process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolific output is not required
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not need to be prolific to gain notice as a short-story author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many successful writers are not constantly publishing. Choose a pace that fits your strengths and process; being prolific may work for some but is not necessary for success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize quality over sheer quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid emphasizing quantity at the cost of quality; focus on editing and letting material rest so you can return with fresh perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors fear work produced under pressure for quantity because it may lack revision and care. It's better to pay attention to what you put out than to push out a high volume of unrefined pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write stories that 'grab' the reader immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft stories that capture a reader (or slush reader) quickly so they will continue reading and recommend/push the piece to editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slush readers are essentially readers; if your story grabs a typical reader it will grab them too. Focus on the elements that hook attention early and sustain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a unique voice—write stories only you could write
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand out by creating stories that come from your own interests and perspective rather than mimicking others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a difference between competent stories (well-constructed but generic) and stories that 'rise above' because they are rooted in the author’s unique voice and obsessions. Those unique stories are more likely to stand out and be memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust your reader instincts over mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on the reading taste you've developed over your life to guide your writing choices rather than trying to copy perceived successful patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors often spend time mimicking technique and produce competent but predictable stories. Instead, interrogate what you are actually interested in and let that inform your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize editorial subjectivity and 'falling in love'
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that editorial decisions often involve subjective enthusiasm—editors/agents can 'fall in love' with a manuscript regardless of author platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform or fame is not required; personal taste and subjective attraction to a piece play a large role in acceptance. This implies some outcomes are unpredictable and not fully 'gameable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission triage and the role of prior credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors/slush processes often triage submissions by prior credits into piles (unknowns, B pile, A list), which affects the order and depth of reads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior publications can move a story into a closer read, but many stories across piles are competent. Expect some randomness: you may sell one story and not others and not be able to fully replicate what worked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research authors’ publication histories to chart a roadmap
rubrics_metrics.description: Track contemporary short fiction authors’ publication histories to learn where they published at various career stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework recommended by the hosts: pick a couple of writers and map where and when they published to get a sense of realistic pathways and market progression.
